questions.problem: What is the trace in the $yz$-plane of the sphere $(x-4)^{2}+{y}^{2}+(z+1)^{2}=25?$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the trace in the $yz$-plane, we substitute $x=0$ into the equation of the sphere:

$$
\begin{aligned}(0-4)^{2}+{y}^{2}+(z+1)^{2} & =25 \\ 16+{y}^{2}+(z+1)^{2} & =25 \\ {y}^{2}+(z+1)^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: What is the projection of the intersection between the sphere ${x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}+(z+1)^{2}=36$ and the plane $z=3$ onto the $xy$-plane.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the intersection of the sphere and the plane $z=3$, we substitute $z=3$ into the equation of the sphere:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}+(3+1)^{2} & =36 \\ {x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2}+16 & =36 \\ {x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =20 \\ {x}^{2}+(y-2)^{2} & =(2\sqrt{5})^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Projecting this onto the $xy$-plane gives us the equation of the circle of radius $2\sqrt{5}$ centered at $(0,2).$

questions.problem: Given the ellipsoid $\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{18}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{8}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{16}=1$, find its intercepts with the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the $x$-intercepts, we plug $y=0$ and $z=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-1)^{2}}{18}+\frac{(0+2)^{2}}{8}+\frac{{0}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{18}+\frac{1}{2}+0 & =1 \\ \frac{(x-1)^{2}}{18} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (x-1)^{2} & =9 \\ x-1 & =\pm 3 \\ x & =1\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solutions $x=4$ and $x=-2.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $x$-axis are $(-2,0,0)$ and $(4,0,0).$

questions.problem: Given the ellipsoid $\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}+(z-1)^{2}=1$, find the domain of $z=z(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
From the ellipsoid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}+(z-1)^{2} & =1 \\ (z-1)^{2} & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4} \\ z-1 & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}-\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}\ge 0 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}\le 1\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the interior of the ellipse $\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}=1$ and its boundary. 

Therefore, the domain is 

$$
{(x,y)\,:\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}\le 1}.
$$

questions.problem: Given the sphere $(x+3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}+(z-4)^{2}=9,$ what is the domain of $z=z(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the equation of the sphere, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}+(z-4)^{2} & =9 \\ (z-4)^{2} & =9-((x+3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}) \\ z-4 & =\pm \sqrt{9-({x}^{2}+(y+3)^{2})} \\ z & =4\pm \sqrt{9-((x+3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}9-((x+3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})\ge 0 \\ (x+3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}\le 9\end{aligned}
$$

This inequality describes the interior and boundary of the circle 

$$
(x+3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=9
$$

which is a circle of radius $3$ centered at $(-3,1)$ in the $xy$-plane.
